summary:
Negeri Sembilan stands under the national framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the federal Penal Code 1936 punish "carnal intercourse against the order of nature" for any person regardless of gender or consent, carrying a maximum of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and apply to visitors. Since the 2018 general election the federal authorities have pursued a crackdown involving arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment under these sections.

Every one of Malaysia's 13 states and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya maintains Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, with cross-dressing and "a man posing as a woman" offences carrying penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. Those state offences reach Muslims only, so a non-Muslim foreign visitor in Negeri Sembilan is exposed to the Penal Code rather than to the Sharia layer.

Negeri Sembilan is the state whose cross-dressing offence was struck down on the record. In November 2014 the Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 of Negeri Sembilan, which criminalised cross-dressing, unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution. The Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor in February 2021 and in Kelantan in February 2024, on the ground that state legislatures lack the power to enact criminal law. Those judgments have narrowed the state layer while leaving the federal Penal Code offences fully intact.

Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters published a joint report on 10 August 2022 documenting state-sponsored discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people in Malaysia, based on interviews with 73 people conducted between 2018 and 2021, among them people living in Negeri Sembilan. The report calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon "rehabilitation" programmes and hostile official rhetoric.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor to Negeri Sembilan the practical exposure is the federal Penal Code: enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted, while the documented pattern across Malaysia is raid-based arrest and public outing. Muslim visitors remain exposed to Sharia offences, which are enforced by state Islamic religious departments and contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing.
tangentialFactors:
The trajectory in Negeri Sembilan runs against the national trend in one respect and with it in another. Section 66 was struck down by the Court of Appeal in November 2014 on federal constitutional grounds, whereas the other states retain their cross-dressing offences; the later Federal Court judgments in Selangor and Kelantan rested on federalism rather than on rights, and left federal criminalisation untouched.

The federal penalty ceiling of 20 years' imprisonment plus whipping is materially heavier than the Sharia maximum of three years, a RM5,000 fine and six strokes of caning, and it applies irrespective of consent, gender or nationality. The Human Dignity Trust records a rise in arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment under the Penal Code sections since the 2018 election, at a moment when the state-level layer has been contracting through litigation.

Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters place Negeri Sembilan within a全国 pattern of state-sponsored discrimination: their 73 interviewees were drawn from across the country between 2018 and 2021, and their recommendations are addressed to lawmakers nationally rather than to any single state administration.
localsOnly:
Section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 had been the instrument used to criminalise cross-dressing by Muslim residents of Negeri Sembilan before the Court of Appeal held it unconstitutional in November 2014. The judgment arose under the Federal Constitution's rights guarantees, and it binds the state's Sharia enforcement apparatus rather than the federal police.

Malaysian Muslim residents remain subject to Sharia codes in every state and federal territory, which typically criminalise same-sex conduct and, in most enactments, cross-dressing. Enforcement is carried out by state Islamic religious departments, and three of the state enactments also bar women from posing as men.

Residents interviewed for the Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters report described discrimination that the organisations attribute to state sponsorship, including the government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats and official rhetoric framing LGBT people as a threat. The report's asks are directed at lawmakers: repeal or strike down the criminal provisions, end the rehabilitation programmes, and stop the hostile framing.

Since 2018 the federal authorities have escalated enforcement under Penal Code sections 377A and 377B through arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment, which affects Malaysian citizens as well as foreign nationals.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Negeri Sembilan state legislature enacted a replacement cross-dressing or gender-presentation offence after section 66 was struck down in November 2014 is not addressed in this source inventory and remains unresolved here.

The sources do not state whether the 2014 Court of Appeal ruling was appealed, complied with in full, or how often the state religious department has continued to act against gender-nonconforming Muslims in Negeri Sembilan since then.

The Human Rights Watch and Justice For Sisters report does not indicate in this inventory how many of its 73 interviewees lived in Negeri Sembilan, so the weight of that testimony for this state specifically is not sourced.

Current arrest and prosecution volumes under sections 377A and 377B within Negeri Sembilan are not given; the only enforcement figures in the parent framework are national or from other states.
